title: How to assess whether your compost is ready to use
subtitle: Simple tests for maturity, stability, and pathogen reduction
excerpt: Home compost varies enormously in quality. Immature compost releases nitrogen as ammonia (damaging to roots), has a pH of 5 to 6, and may contain weed seeds or pathogens. Mature compost smells earthy, has pH 6.5 to 7.5, and supports plant growth. A handful of simple checks, smell, appearance, temperature, and a germination test, tells you whether your batch is ready or needs more time.
sourceNotes: RHS composting and compost maturity guidance 2024. WRAP MDD025 maturity index for home-produced compost. Standardised Compost Maturity Index (CCME 2005) adapted for home use.

content.text: The most common mistake with home compost is using it too early. Partially composted material contains phytotoxic compounds, mainly volatile fatty acids and high concentrations of ammonia nitrogen, that inhibit seed germination and damage fine roots. A batch dug into a raised bed in spring that looks dark and decomposed may have had its greens added 8 weeks ago without enough turning to complete the process. The plants that go in will stall or fail.

Take a handful from the centre of the heap and smell it closely. Mature compost smells like forest floor, earthy, slightly sweet, clean. Immature compost smells of ammonia (sharp, eye-watering), silage (sweet-sour, vinegary), or sulphur (rotten egg). Any of these off-notes means the material needs more time or turning before use.

Mature compost is dark brown to black, crumbly, and shows no recognisable original materials. You should not be able to identify vegetable peelings, grass clippings, or paper. Twigs and eggshells are exceptions, they take longer to break down and their presence does not indicate immaturity elsewhere. If you can identify most of the original inputs, the material is not ready.

A mature heap is no longer generating heat. Insert a compost thermometer to the centre. If the temperature is more than 5°C above ambient, the material is still in an active decomposition phase, apply it now and it may generate heat and ammonia in the soil. Leave it to complete the cycle.
Take two equal-sized pots or trays. Fill one with the compost to be tested. Fill the other with bought potting compost or garden soil (the control).
Press 10 cress seeds into each tray at an equal depth (roughly 5 mm). Water both lightly and keep in the same conditions.

After 5 days, count germinated seeds and compare seedling height. If germination in the test compost is 70% or more of the control, the material is mature. If germination is less than 50% of the control, the compost has phytotoxic compounds and needs more time.
If the compost fails the test

Turn the heap, add more carbon if the smell is ammoniacal, water if it is dry, and leave for a further 4 to 6 weeks. Re-test before using. Do not use failing compost around seeds or seedlings, it can be applied to bare fallow soil in autumn to finish composting in place, where the phytotoxins will dissipate before spring planting.
